fr:title.text: GQA saves cache, not projection FLOPs

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: GQA saves cache, not projection FLOPs

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Per layer, what do the QKVO projections cost in parameters and training FLOPs under Group Query Attention with N query heads, K key/value heads, and head dimension H?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Parameters: 2D(N+K)H, from W_Q[D,N,H] and W_O[N,H,D] at DNH each, plus W_K, W_V[D,K,H] at DKH each.
Training FLOPs: 12BTD(N+K)H — each projection is 6BTD \cdot (\text {heads}) \cdot H.
The variants are one knob. K = N is plain multi-head attention; K = 1 is MQA; 1 < K < N with K \mid N is grouped-query, with group size G = N/K.
Read the formula for what shrinking K actually buys. It touches only the K term, so the projection cost falls from 2N to N + K — at most a factor of two, and usually far less. That is not why anyone uses GQA. The payoff is the KV-cache, which scales with K alone and is the binding constraint at generation time.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: An AllGather gets resources from all devices onto one device. In TPU's Ring topology, this is done in \frac {N}{2} hops via each TPU sending its shard to the neighboring chip.

Assuming we have X shards and the total bytes is N, then each chip must send \frac {N}{X} bytes. If we have an ICI bandwidth of W_{\text {ICI}}, then for each chip to send to its neighbor will be T_{1\text { hop}} = \frac {N}{X\cdot W_{\text {ICI}}} Now each chip must send across X hops, which gives T = X\cdot T_{1\text { hop}} = \frac {N}{W_{\text {ICI}}}.This does not change if we use the bi-directional bandwidth because then we have 2N bytes but only need to send at most \frac {X}{2} hops!
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. A super fun trick from [scaling-book, Ex 3.2]: If you have an unused replicated dimension, then you can shard the replicated axis and perform an AllGather over both dimensions to double your bandwidth!

fr:title.text: AllGather costs the same at any device count

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: AllGather costs the same at any device count

fr:mainmatter.html:p: AllGather: signature, mechanism, and cost?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:p: Signature [A_X, B] \to [A, B] — it removes a subscript, reassembling shards so every device on that axis holds a full copy. It can drop just one of several axes: A[I_{XY}, J] \to A[I_Y, J].
Mechanism: pass each shard around the ring, N-1 hops in one direction or about N/2 bidirectionally.

Cost, when bandwidth-bound: T = V / W_{\mathrm {ici}} on bidirectional bandwidth, or V / (W_{\mathrm {ici}} \cdot N_{\mathrm {axes}}) across several mesh axes. The takeaway is that this is independent of the device count X — each hop sends V/X bytes but you make X/2 hops. Only array size and link bandwidth matter.

Latency-bound regime: about 1\mu \mathrm {s} intrinsic cost per hop, so T = \max (T_{\min } \cdot \sum _i |X_i| / 2,\; V / (W \cdot N_{\mathrm {axes}})). On v5e (4.5e10 unidirectional) anything under ~45 kB is latency-bound.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Sharded matmul, case 2: one multiplicand has a sharded contracting dimension, A[I, J_X] \cdot B[J, K] \to C[I, K]. Which primitive, and what is the alternative?

html:div.html:details:
Answer AllGather the sharded input first, then matmul locally: \mathrm {AllGather}_X(A[I, J_X]) \to A[I, J], then A[I, J] \cdot B[J, K] \to C[I, K]. You cannot just multiply the local shards, because the sum over J is split across X and each device holds only a partial sum.
The alternative is to treat it like case 3: do the local partial matmul and AllReduce or ReduceScatter the result. That shards the FLOPs but usually costs more comms. For X[B,D] \cdot Y[D_X,F], the gather moves 2DF bytes and the reduce moves 2 \cdot 2BF, so the reduce path wins roughly when D > 2B.
Rare in practice, though — the other input is usually sharded along the same axis anyway, as under FSDP.

fr:title.text: A mesh axis may appear only once

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A mesh axis may appear only once

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Sharded matmul, case 4: both multiplicands have a non-contracting dimension sharded along the same mesh axis, A[I_X, J] \cdot B[J, K_X]. Why is this invalid, and how do you resolve it?

html:div.html:details:
Answer A mesh axis may appear at most once in a sharding. Writing C[I_X, K_X] would give shard i only the (i,i) block — the block diagonal. The off-diagonal blocks of C exist nowhere, so the result is unrecoverable.
The fix is to AllGather one of the two inputs along X first, so that X appears once in the output:
\mathrm {AllGather}_X(A) \to A[I, J], giving C[I, K_X].
\mathrm {AllGather}_X(B) \to B[J, K], giving C[I_X, K].
Which one you pick is decided by the sharding the downstream ops want.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: When the correctness of a program depends on the order in which concurrent Threads schedule, you have a race condition. The classic example: two threads each execute

html:pre.html:code: mov addr reg // load add 1 reg // increment mov reg addr // store

fr:mainmatter.html:p: intending to increment a shared variable twice. If the OS interleaves the threads at the wrong instruction boundary:
The result is a single increment, not two — both threads loaded the same starting value and the second store clobbered the first.
The fix is to prevent interleaving inside the code region that touches shared state — the Critical section — using a synchronization primitive like Locks.

A fair spin lock based on two counters. Each arriving thread takes a "ticket" by atomically incrementing next_ticket and then spins until now_serving equals its ticket. Release simply increments now_serving. Threads acquire the lock in FIFO order, which prevents starvation but does not by itself reduce contention.

html:pre.html:code:
acquire(lock_ptr): my_ticket = fetch_and_increment(lock_ptr->next_ticket) while (lock_ptr->now_serving != my_ticket); // spin
release(lock_ptr): lock_ptr->now_serving = lock_ptr->now_serving + 1

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Problem. Still O(n) coherence traffic on release: incrementing now_serving invalidates the line on every waiter, and they all reload it to recheck their ticket.

fr:title.text: Matching contracting shards give partial sums

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Matching contracting shards give partial sums

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Sharded matmul, case 3: both multiplicands are sharded along the contracting dimension on the same mesh axis, A[I, J_X] \cdot B[J_X, K]. What happens, and which primitive fixes it?

html:div.html:details:
Answer The local shards can be multiplied — they share contracting indices — but each device ends up with only a partial sum, written C[I, K]\{U_X\}, "unreduced along X":
A \cdot B = \sum _i A[:,i] \otimes B[i,:]
Device i owns the i-th column block of A and the i-th row block of B, so it computes exactly the i-th term of that sum.
The fix is AllReduce along X for a replicated C[I, K] — or the cheaper \mathrm {ReduceScatter}_{X,K} \to C[I, K_X] if you can leave the output sharded. That is half the cost, and defers the gather, possibly forever.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The keys and values of every token seen so far, held in memory across decoding steps so that each is projected once rather than once per step. Attention at step t needs k_j and v_j for every j \le t, and each of those is a function of token j and the weights alone — nothing about it depends on t. So it is computable once and never again, and the only real question is whether you will spend memory to avoid recomputing it.

The cost of not spending it is quadratic, which is easy to miss because per step it looks merely linear: admitting token t means rebuilding t+1 key–value pairs, so a sequence of S tokens costs \sum _{t=1}^{S} t = S(S+1)/2 projections rather than S. The query is the asymmetry that makes the trade available at all — only the newest position needs one, so q_t is a single row either way, and decoding is a matrix–vector product against a K and V that grow by one row a step.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Notation. Following the scaling book: S is the KV sequence length, K the number of key/value heads, H the head dimension, L the layers, B the batch. The clash between K as a matrix and K as a head count is unfortunate and universal.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: What the cache costs is memory, and the shape of that cost is the reason it governs inference planning. Each token contributes a key and a value in every layer, so a batch holds

which is linear in the sequence length and — unlike the weights — per sequence, so it cannot be amortised over the batch. Context length and batch size are therefore drawn from the same High bandwidth memory budget, and past a certain context the cache dominates residency outright, which is Processing in Memory for ML's framing of the memory wall.

It also decides what decoding is bound by. At step t the model streams the entire cache through the Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU) to do O(S) multiply-accumulates against a single query row, so the Arithmetic intensity is roughly one FLOP per byte read — far below the ridge point of any accelerator, and flat in S. Decoding is bandwidth-bound, and the cache is what it is bound by.

Every fix for that attacks a factor in the expression above rather than the idea of caching. MQA sets K = 1 and shares one key/value head across all query heads; Group Query Attention sets it to a group count and interpolates; Sliding Window Attention bounds S instead by refusing to attend past a window. The FLOPs are unchanged in all three — what changes is how many bytes have to move to supply them.

fr:title.text: The KV cache scales with K, and is per-sequence

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The KV cache scales with K, and is per-sequence

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How large is a KV-cache, and which dimension actually drives it?

html:div.html:details:
Answer The cache has shape [2, S, L, K, H] per sequence — the leading 2 is keys and values — so in int8 it is 2SLKH bytes.
Worked: S = 8\mathrm {k}, L = 64, KH = D = 8192 gives 2 \cdot 8192 \cdot 64 \cdot 8192 \approx 8 GiB for a single sequence.
Two things in that expression decide inference planning. It scales with K, the number of key/value heads, and not with the N query heads — which is the whole argument for Group Query Attention and MQA at K \ll N. And it is per sequence, so unlike the weights it cannot be amortised over the batch: it competes with batch size for the same High bandwidth memory budget, and generation is bandwidth-bound on streaming it.

fr:title.text: Arithmetic intensity and the ridge point

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Arithmetic intensity and the ridge point

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Define arithmetic intensity and derive the test for whether an op is compute-bound.

fr:title.text: The batch size is the intensity

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The batch size is the intensity

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For a bf16 matmul [B, D] \times [D, F] \to [B, F], give the FLOPs, bytes, intensity, and the resulting rule of thumb.

html:div.html:details:
Answer \text {FLOPs} = 2BDF and \text {bytes} = 2BD + 2DF + 2BF — both operands loaded, the output written, two bytes apiece — so
\mathrm {Intensity} = \frac {BDF}{BD + DF + BF}
With B \ll D, F the DF term dominates the denominator and the intensity collapses to BDF / DF = B. The whole rule of thumb is that the batch size is the intensity: a matmul is compute-bound once the per-replica batch exceeds 240 tokens on TPU (\approx 295 on H100, from 9.89 \times 10^{14} / 3.35 \times 10^{12}).
Three caveats. B counts tokens, not sequences. The threshold is per replica — sharding scales FLOPs and bandwidth together, so it applies to each copy of the weights (Data parallelism). And tiling changes the byte count once the matmul is large enough that the operands no longer fit.

fr:title.text: Constant intensity of a dot product

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Constant intensity of a dot product

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Why is a dot product x \cdot y essentially always comms-bound?

html:div.html:details:
Answer For \mathrm {bf16}[N] \times \mathrm {bf16}[N] \to \mathrm {bf16}[1] the work is N multiplies and N - 1 adds while the traffic is 2N + 2N + 2 bytes, so
\mathrm {Intensity} = \frac {2N - 1}{4N + 2} \longrightarrow \frac {1}{2}
The point is that the intensity is constant in N: there is no size you can grow into to escape it, unlike a matmul whose intensity rises with the batch. Half a FLOP per byte sits far below any ridge point — even the TPU v5p VPU, at roughly 7 \times 10^{12} FLOPs/s per core, wants an intensity near 3.
Reuse is what buys intensity. Every byte loaded into a matmul feeds many FLOPs; in a dot product it feeds one.

fr:title.text: Weight-only int8 halves the compute-bound batch

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Weight-only int8 halves the compute-bound batch

fr:mainmatter.html:p: With weights in int8 but activations and compute in bf16, at what batch size does a matmul become compute-bound?

html:div.html:details:
Answer For \mathrm {bf16}[B, D] \times \mathrm {int8}[D, F] \to \mathrm {bf16}[B, F] the FLOPs are unchanged at 2BDF and still run at the bf16 rate of 1.97 \times 10^{14}, but the weights now cost DF bytes instead of 2DF. With B small the intensity therefore roughly doubles to 2B, and
2B > 240 \implies B > 120
Half the usual threshold — weight-only int8 quantization is an easy win even on hardware you are not using in int8.
Contrast full int8, weights and OPs: the intensity is again \approx 2B, but the ridge point doubles too, to 3.94 \times 10^{14} / 8.2 \times 10^{11} = 480, so B > 240 — unchanged. What full int8 buys is wall-clock at a given batch, not a smaller batch.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is the arithmetic intensity of [B, D] \times [B, D, F] \to [B, F] — a separate weight matrix per batch element — and what is the lesson?

html:div.html:details:
Answer In int8, the work is the same 2BDF — these are B independent [D] \times [D, F] products — but the traffic is BD + BDF + BF, dominated by the BDF weight term. So
\mathrm {Intensity} = \frac {2BDF}{BD + BDF + BF} \approx 2
constant. Batching bought nothing: B appears in numerator and denominator and cancels, leaving you comms-bound at every batch size.
The lesson is that a matmul's intensity comes entirely from amortizing one weight load across many tokens. Give every token its own weights and the amortization disappears — which is why per-example weights, and anything shaped like them, never reach the flat roof.

fr:title.text: The sharded-matmul threshold falls on D, not B

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The sharded-matmul threshold falls on D, not B

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two chips split X[B, D] and Y[D, F] along D, each computing a partial sum and exchanging it. When is this compute-bound, and why is the threshold surprising?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Each chip does half the contraction, T_{\mathrm {math}} = BDF / 1.97 \times 10^{14}, then ships its [B, F] partial sum across the interconnect, T_{\mathrm {comms}} = 2BF / 4.5 \times 10^{10}. Compute-bound means
\frac {BDF}{2BF} = \frac {D}{2} > \frac {1.97 \times 10^{14}}{4.5 \times 10^{10}} = 4377 \implies D > 8755
The surprise is that the threshold depends on D, not B: the batch scales FLOPs and bytes-sent identically and cancels out. Same roofline machinery as a single-chip matmul, but because the relevant bandwidth is now the network, a different dimension decides whether Tensor Parallelism pays for itself — the contracted dimension has to be large enough to hide the exchange.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: VMEM vs HBM bandwidth: what is the ratio, and what does it do to the roofline?

html:div.html:details:
Answer VMEM\to MXU bandwidth is roughly 22\times HBM bandwidth, so the critical arithmetic intensity for peak FLOPs drops from ~240 to ~10–20.
Worked, with int8[16384,4096] weights on v5e: FLOPs-bound at B > 267 out of HBM, but only B > 11 out of VMEM — call it 20 in practice, since you cannot spend all of VMEM's bandwidth on weights.
The consequence is VMEM prefetch: load the FFW weights during attention and the load disappears behind compute. The limit is capacity — VMEM is tiny, so a layer's weights have to be small or sharded enough to fit with room to spare.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A grid of processing elements in which every operand moves by one hop per cycle to a fixed neighbour, and nothing is addressed. A PE multiplies what arrives at it, adds what arrived from above, and passes the result on. There is no register file to name, no arbitration, and no scheduler: the dataflow is the wiring, and the only freedom in the design is which of the three operands you decide to hold still.

Hold the output still and each PE owns one entry of the result, accumulating in place while both inputs stream past. Hold the weights still — the choice the Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU) makes — and each PE pins one w_{ij} for the whole tile while activations stream in from the left and partial sums fall downward. The second is the one worth being able to draw from memory, because the staggering it requires is where every systolic-array bubble comes from:

The stagger is the whole trick. Row i of the activation tape is held back i cycles, so that x_k arrives at PE(k, j) on precisely the cycle the running sum for column j reaches that row. The set of PEs firing on cycle t is therefore the anti-diagonal i + j = t, and a finished dot product falls out of the bottom of column j having been accumulated on the way down — never written to memory, never read back.
What you pay for that is the fill and the drain. An N \times N array streaming M samples is busy for M + 2N - 2 cycles but does only M N^2 useful multiply-accumulates, so utilisation is

For the four-by-four array above, four samples give 40%. On a real 128 \times 128 MXU the fill is 2N - 2 = 254 cycles, so one isolated 8 \times 128 tile — the shape of the native op — would run at 8/262, near three per cent. That number is not what the hardware achieves, and the gap is the point: consecutive tiles stream in back-to-back with no bubble between them, so the fill is paid once per run of matmuls rather than once per tile. This is the fill bubble, and it is why the cost of a small matmul is dominated by a fixed charge that a large one amortises away.

The native op is one bf16[8,128] @ bf16[128,128] -> f32[8,128] every 8 cycles, or about 5e13 bf16 FLOPs/s per MXU at 1.5 GHz. A v5e chip has enough MXUs to reach ~2e14.

fr:title.text: Why the MXU pads everything to 128

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why the MXU pads everything to 128

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is the native op of one Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU), and why does that force padding to 128?

html:div.html:details:
Answer One bf16[8,128] @ bf16[128,128] -> f32[8,128] every 8 cycles, on a 128 \times 128 systolic array — 256 \times 256 on v6e/Trillium.
The array's side length is fixed in hardware, so any matrix axis shorter than 128 (256 on v6e) is padded up to it, and the FLOPs spent on the padding are simply wasted. With 2–4 MXUs per core, tiling dimensions want to exceed 128 \times the MXU count.
Scale: roughly 5e13 bf16 FLOPs/s per MXU at 1.5 GHz, so about 2e14 per v5e chip. int8 runs ~2\times faster, int4 ~4\times .

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Sketch the dataflow through a 128 \times 128 systolic array (Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU)). Where does the pipeline bubble come from?

html:div.html:details:
Answer A 2D grid of 16,384 ALUs, each doing one multiply-add per cycle.
Weights (RHS, 128 \times 128) are pushed down from the top.
Activations (LHS, 8 \times 128) stream in from the left.
Each cell multiplies its overlapped pair, adds the partial sum arriving from above, and passes the result down.
The bubble: both operands are loaded diagonally, so the array needs a fill period before every cell is busy. Once filled, new LHS/RHS stream in back-to-back with no further bubble — which is why large matrices amortize the fill and small ones do not.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A core component of the TPU architecture responsible for elementwise operations.

html:ul.html:li: 2D SIMD execution, where each of 1024 sites execute same program in lockstep.
Each site contains 4 ALUs, enabling 4096 FLOPs.
Fed a 8x128 Vector Register in one cycle.

fr:title.text: The VPU is thirty times smaller than the MXU

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The VPU is thirty times smaller than the MXU

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Vector Processing Unit: what is its shape and throughput relative to the Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU), and which reductions are cheap?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Shape (8\ \text {sublanes}, 128\ \text {lanes}), with 4 independent ALUs per position and most ops at 1/cycle:
8 \times 128 \times 4 \times 1.75\mathrm {e}9 \approx 7\mathrm {e}12 \text { FLOPs/s}
on v5p — about 30\times less than the ~2e14 MXU FLOPs/s per core. VPU work is fp32.
Reductions along the sublane axis (the 8) are cheap: an intra-lane shuffle by 4/2/1 plus three pairwise adds. Cross-lane reductions need the separate XLU, which is slow and expensive.
Control is skewed the other way: a single scalar core fetches and dispatches everything and can issue only one DMA request per cycle. Efficient, but it blocks data-dependent vectorization.

fr:title.text: The three units and the one data path

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The three units and the one data path

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What are the three units inside a TPU TensorCore (TPU), and what is the data path from HBM to compute?

html:div.html:details:
Answer
MXU — matrix multiply on a systolic array. Nearly all of the FLOPs.
VPU — elementwise ops (ReLU, add, mul) and reductions.
VMEM — an on-chip scratchpad in the TensorCore, like L1/L2 but far larger (~128 MiB on v5e) and programmer-controlled rather than a cache.
The path is HBM \to VMEM \to VREGs \to MXU/VPU \to VMEM \to HBM. Nothing computes directly out of HBM. All of it is pipelined — the copies overlap with MXU work, so the array never stalls waiting on memory.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Name the four communication tiers on a TPU, fastest to slowest, with per-chip v5p numbers.

html:div.html:details:
Answer
HBM \leftrightarrow TensorCore — 2.8e12 B/s.
ICI (Inter-chip interconnect, chip to nearest neighbors) — 9e10 B/s per axis one-way, across 3 axes on v5p.
PCIe (host to its tray of chips) — 1.6e10 B/s, about 100\times slower than HBM.
DCN (host to host) — 6.25e9 B/s.
The design rule that falls out: keep the bytes crossing each channel proportional to that channel's speed. Note also that a TPU\to TPU transfer over DCN pays the whole chain — PCIe, NIC egress, NIC ingress, PCIe again.

fr:title.text: Which TPU axes actually wrap around

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Which TPU axes actually wrap around

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Inter-chip interconnect topology: which generations get which torus, and when do you actually get wraparound links?

html:div.html:details:
Answer
2D torus, 4 neighbors — v2, v3, v5e, v6e. A pod caps at 16 \times 16; past that, pods talk over DCN.
3D torus, 6 neighbors — v4, v5p. Superpods are 16 \times 16 \times 16 (v4) and 16 \times 20 \times 28 (v5p), built from reconfigurable 4 \times 4 \times 4 cubes joined by optical links.
Wraparounds exist only on full-cube multiples (4 \times 4 \times 4, 4 \times 4 \times 8 — not 2 \times 2 \times 4, since the optical switches only exist on a full cube), or on a v5e/v6e axis of exactly 16, so an 8 \times 16 slice wraps the long axis only. Losing the wraparound roughly doubles comms time.
Links are nearest-neighbor only and bypass the hosts entirely, so distant chips hop through the chips between them — unlike a GPU's switch hierarchy.

fr:title.text: Sharded Matrices and How to Multiply Them

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Sharded Matrices and How to Multiply Them

fr:title.text: An unsharded contracting axis needs no comms

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: An unsharded contracting axis needs no comms

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Sharded matmul, case 1: neither multiplicand has a sharded contracting dimension. What communication is required, and what is the output sharding?

html:div.html:details:
Answer None at all. Each device does a local block matmul and the result is already sharded correctly:
A[I_X, J] \cdot B[J, K_Y] \to C[I_X, K_Y]
The contracting axis J is unsharded, so every device holds complete contracting slices and the computation does not depend on the sharding. The output simply inherits the input shardings.
The one caveat: this holds only if the two inputs' non-contracting dimensions are not sharded over the same mesh axis — that case is invalid.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: An AllGather gets resources from all devices onto one device. In TPU's Ring topology, this is done in \frac {N}{2} hops via each TPU sending its shard to the neighboring chip.

Assuming we have X shards and the total bytes is N, then each chip must send \frac {N}{X} bytes. If we have an ICI bandwidth of W_{\text {ICI}}, then for each chip to send to its neighbor will be T_{1\text { hop}} = \frac {N}{X\cdot W_{\text {ICI}}} Now each chip must send across X hops, which gives T = X\cdot T_{1\text { hop}} = \frac {N}{W_{\text {ICI}}}.This does not change if we use the bi-directional bandwidth because then we have 2N bytes but only need to send at most \frac {X}{2} hops!
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. A super fun trick from [scaling-book, Ex 3.2]: If you have an unused replicated dimension, then you can shard the replicated axis and perform an AllGather over both dimensions to double your bandwidth!

fr:title.text: AllGather costs the same at any device count

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: AllGather costs the same at any device count

fr:mainmatter.html:p: AllGather: signature, mechanism, and cost?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:p: Signature [A_X, B] \to [A, B] — it removes a subscript, reassembling shards so every device on that axis holds a full copy. It can drop just one of several axes: A[I_{XY}, J] \to A[I_Y, J].
Mechanism: pass each shard around the ring, N-1 hops in one direction or about N/2 bidirectionally.

Cost, when bandwidth-bound: T = V / W_{\mathrm {ici}} on bidirectional bandwidth, or V / (W_{\mathrm {ici}} \cdot N_{\mathrm {axes}}) across several mesh axes. The takeaway is that this is independent of the device count X — each hop sends V/X bytes but you make X/2 hops. Only array size and link bandwidth matter.

Latency-bound regime: about 1\mu \mathrm {s} intrinsic cost per hop, so T = \max (T_{\min } \cdot \sum _i |X_i| / 2,\; V / (W \cdot N_{\mathrm {axes}})). On v5e (4.5e10 unidirectional) anything under ~45 kB is latency-bound.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Sharded matmul, case 2: one multiplicand has a sharded contracting dimension, A[I, J_X] \cdot B[J, K] \to C[I, K]. Which primitive, and what is the alternative?

html:div.html:details:
Answer AllGather the sharded input first, then matmul locally: \mathrm {AllGather}_X(A[I, J_X]) \to A[I, J], then A[I, J] \cdot B[J, K] \to C[I, K]. You cannot just multiply the local shards, because the sum over J is split across X and each device holds only a partial sum.
The alternative is to treat it like case 3: do the local partial matmul and AllReduce or ReduceScatter the result. That shards the FLOPs but usually costs more comms. For X[B,D] \cdot Y[D_X,F], the gather moves 2DF bytes and the reduce moves 2 \cdot 2BF, so the reduce path wins roughly when D > 2B.
Rare in practice, though — the other input is usually sharded along the same axis anyway, as under FSDP.

fr:title.text: A mesh axis may appear only once

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A mesh axis may appear only once

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Sharded matmul, case 4: both multiplicands have a non-contracting dimension sharded along the same mesh axis, A[I_X, J] \cdot B[J, K_X]. Why is this invalid, and how do you resolve it?

html:div.html:details:
Answer A mesh axis may appear at most once in a sharding. Writing C[I_X, K_X] would give shard i only the (i,i) block — the block diagonal. The off-diagonal blocks of C exist nowhere, so the result is unrecoverable.
The fix is to AllGather one of the two inputs along X first, so that X appears once in the output:
\mathrm {AllGather}_X(A) \to A[I, J], giving C[I, K_X].
\mathrm {AllGather}_X(B) \to B[J, K], giving C[I_X, K].
Which one you pick is decided by the sharding the downstream ops want.

fr:title.text: Matching contracting shards give partial sums

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Matching contracting shards give partial sums

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Sharded matmul, case 3: both multiplicands are sharded along the contracting dimension on the same mesh axis, A[I, J_X] \cdot B[J_X, K]. What happens, and which primitive fixes it?

html:div.html:details:
Answer The local shards can be multiplied — they share contracting indices — but each device ends up with only a partial sum, written C[I, K]\{U_X\}, "unreduced along X":
A \cdot B = \sum _i A[:,i] \otimes B[i,:]
Device i owns the i-th column block of A and the i-th row block of B, so it computes exactly the i-th term of that sum.
The fix is AllReduce along X for a replicated C[I, K] — or the cheaper \mathrm {ReduceScatter}_{X,K} \to C[I, K_X] if you can leave the output sharded. That is half the cost, and defers the gather, possibly forever.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The collective that resolves partial sums along a mesh axis and leaves the result sharded rather than replicated: [A, B]\{U_X\} \to [A_X, B]. It is the reduction half of an AllReduce, and the transpose of an AllGather. Same ring pass, same cost V / W_{\mathrm {ici}}, except each device sums the shard arriving from its left neighbour into its own copy instead of merely keeping it.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Notation. Because it introduces a subscript, you have to say where it goes: \mathrm {ReduceScatter}_{X,K} reduces along mesh axis X and shards the result along K. That freedom is the whole argument for preferring it. Namely, whenever the consumer can accept a sharded input, stopping at the ReduceScatter costs half what an AllReduce does and defers the gather, possibly forever.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The mechanism is easiest to see as a schedule. Each device starts holding a full-size buffer that is only a partial sum, and on every step forwards one chunk rightward and folds in the chunk arriving from its left. After N-1 steps device b holds chunk b summed over all N partials and has forwarded the rest away, which is also why the resident memory falls by N.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Question. How do we know what chunk to send to who?

html:div.html:details: Answer.It is actually remarkably easy. If there are N devices, then you just compute which device is N - 1 hops away from you. You send that chunk to your right neighbor. Each chunk then propagates through the ring and will end up with the completed chunked sum on the correct device

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Note that the steps are not N-1 rounds of moving a whole buffer: every link carries one chunk in the same direction at the same time, so the cost is N-1 chunk-times, and the N in the chunk size cancels the N-1 in the step count. Nothing is ever broadcast, which is the sense in which the ring is optimal and the reason a ReduceScatter is not merely an AllReduce with a slice at the end.
ReduceScatter: signature, relationship to AllGather, and cost?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Signature [A, B]\{U_X\} \to [A_X, B] — it resolves partial sums along X and leaves the result sharded along a dimension of your choosing. It introduces a subscript, which is why you have to say where: \mathrm {ReduceScatter}_{X,K}.
Mechanism: the same ring pass as an AllGather, except you sum the incoming shards instead of keeping them. Cost is therefore identical, V / W_{\mathrm {ici}}.
Duality: AllGather and ReduceScatter are transposes of each other, hence each other's derivative — an AllGather in the forward pass means a ReduceScatter on the reverse-mode gradients, and vice versa. (Broadcast is u \otimes I, reduce is u^\top \otimes I.)

fr:title.text: AllReduce is two collectives, not one

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: AllReduce is two collectives, not one

fr:mainmatter.html:p: AllReduce: signature, decomposition, and cost relative to an AllGather?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Signature [A_X, B]\{U_Y\} \to [A_X, B] — it removes the "unreduced" suffix, leaving every device on the axis holding the same fully-summed value, unsharded along Y.
It is not really a primitive: an AllReduce is a ReduceScatter followed by an AllGather.
A[I_X, J]\{U_Y\} \xrightarrow {\ \mathrm {ReduceScatter}_{Y,J}\ } A[I_X, J_Y] \xrightarrow {\ \mathrm {AllGather}_Y\ } A[I_X, J]
Cost 2V / W_{\mathrm {ici}}, exactly 2\times an AllGather — which is the practical argument for stopping at the ReduceScatter whenever the consumer can accept a sharded output. The AllGather can then be deferred, or skipped entirely.

fr:title.text: AllToAll is a quarter of an AllGather

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: AllToAll is a quarter of an AllGather

fr:mainmatter.html:p: AllToAll: signature, when it shows up, and why is it cheaper than an AllGather?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Signature [A, B_X] \to [A_X, B] — a sharded transposition, which moves a subscript from one logical axis to another.
When: never out of a sharded matmul. It is for resharding between regions of a computation with incompatible layouts — classically MoE routing.
Cost V \cdot \max (A, B, C, \ldots ) / (4 N W_{\mathrm {ici}}); on a 1D mesh that is V / (4 W_{\mathrm {ici}}), a quarter of an AllGather, and it scales down further in 2D+ with the shortest axis.
Why cheaper, as 2 \times 2: each device need not send its whole shard everywhere, so the sum becomes D + (D-1) + \cdots + 1 instead of D repeated D times — a factor of 2. And bidirectionality buys 4\times here rather than the 2\times it buys an AllGather, since blocks travel at most D/2 hops in either direction. Equivalently: two random nodes on a ring are about N/4 hops apart.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The four collectives that sharded matmuls actually need, in the [scaling-book] notation: a subscript is a mesh axis the array is split along, and \{U_X\} marks an array that is unreduced along X — every device holds a full-size partial sum. A collective is then a rewrite of that decoration, and its cost is a function of how many bytes have to cross the ICI to do it.

html:tr.html:td: Gathers all the shards of a sharded array along an axis, removing a subscript.
Sums a partially summed array along an axis and shards it along another axis, adding a subscript.
Sums a partially summed array along an axis, removing the \{U_X\}. Combines an AllGather and a ReduceScatter.
Gathers (replicates) an axis and shards a different dimension along the same axis.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Only two of these are primitives. An AllReduce is a ReduceScatter followed by an AllGather, which is exactly why it costs twice as much, and the practical consequence is that you should stop at the ReduceScatter whenever the consumer can accept a sharded input. AllGather and ReduceScatter are transposes of each other and hence each other's derivative, so a forward-pass AllGather implies a ReduceScatter on the reverse-mode gradients.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. The runtime column is written relative to the AllGather because every entry is the same ring pass over the same V bytes — the only thing that changes is how far each byte travels. An AllToAll is 4\times cheaper because a shard's destination is on average a quarter of the ring away rather than all the way around, and no byte is broadcast to every device [scaling-book, Ex 3.10]. The \text {num\_axes} factor in the AllGather row is the trick from [scaling-book, Ex 3.2]: gathering over two mesh axes at once buys you both axes' bandwidth.

Remark. Notice what is absent from the runtime column: the number of devices. A ring collective moves V bytes off each chip regardless of how big the ring is, so cost depends on the array and the link, not the mesh size, which is what makes these affordable at pod scale and why the roofline question is comms-vs-FLOPs rather than comms-vs-devices.

fr:title.text: Every axis label appears once in the FLOP count

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Every axis label appears once in the FLOP count

fr:mainmatter.html:p: An einsum contracts C[GHIJKL] with D[GHMNKL], where GH are batching axes and KL are contracting axes. How many FLOPs?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Two times the product of every distinct label, each counted once:
2 \cdot GH \cdot IJ \cdot MN \cdot KL
Why. Every output element is a dot product over the contracted axes, and a dot product spends one multiply and one add per term — that is the factor of two. The batch axes index independent subproblems, so they multiply the total work but appear only once in the product, exactly as the contracted axes do.
The vocabulary is what makes the rule mechanical. A contracting label appears in both inputs and is absent from the output; a batching label appears in both inputs and the output. Everything else is a free axis of one input. Once the labels are sorted that way, the count is read off the einsum string without thinking about the shape of the loop nest.
Caveat. With no contracting axes there is no dot product — the operation is an elementwise product, and the factor of two goes away.

fr:title.text: The backward pass is two matmuls, not one

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The backward pass is two matmuls, not one

fr:mainmatter.html:p: One matmul C = AB with A[N,P], B[P,M] costs 2NPM FLOPs at inference but 6NPM in training. Where do the other two thirds come from?

html:div.html:details:
Answer The forward pass contracts over P and costs 2NPM. Backpropagation then needs two matmuls of exactly that size, not one:
\partial L/\partial B = A^{\top }(\partial L/\partial C), contracting over N — the parameter gradient;
\partial L/\partial A = (\partial L/\partial C)B^{\top }, contracting over M — not a parameter gradient at all, but the signal handed to earlier layers.
Each of the three contracts a different axis of the same N \times P \times M box, so each costs 2NPM and the total is 6NPM, three times the forward pass. It is easy to remember only the first backward matmul and land on 4NPM; the activation gradient is the one that goes missing.
Why the constant is worth memorising. PM is the parameter count of that matrix and N is the token count, so 6NPM is precisely the 6 \cdot \mathrm {params} \cdot \mathrm {tokens} rule of thumb — the whole training cost of a Transformer is a sum of such terms.

fr:title.text: Gating splits the up-projection in two

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Gating splits the up-projection in two

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For one Transformer layer with a gated MLP, what are the parameter count and training FLOPs — and why is the coefficient three rather than two?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Parameters: 3DF, from W_{in1}[D,F], W_{in2}[D,F], W_{out}[F,D].
Training FLOPs: 18BTDF — three matmuls at 6BTDF each, by the 6NPM rule.
Where the third matrix comes from. A Gated Linear Unit (GLU) splits the up-projection into two matrices whose outputs are multiplied elementwise, \sigma (AW_{in1}) \odot (AW_{in2}), so one of them acts as a gate on the other. LLaMA, DeepSeek and most current models do this. A non-gated MLP has a single W_{in} and so 2DF params — and typically scales D and F up to compensate, which is why the two families cost about the same at equal quality.
The gate itself is O(BTF) — elementwise, no contraction, and negligible against BTDF.

fr:title.text: GQA saves cache, not projection FLOPs

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: GQA saves cache, not projection FLOPs

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Per layer, what do the QKVO projections cost in parameters and training FLOPs under Group Query Attention with N query heads, K key/value heads, and head dimension H?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Parameters: 2D(N+K)H, from W_Q[D,N,H] and W_O[N,H,D] at DNH each, plus W_K, W_V[D,K,H] at DKH each.
Training FLOPs: 12BTD(N+K)H — each projection is 6BTD \cdot (\text {heads}) \cdot H.
The variants are one knob. K = N is plain multi-head attention; K = 1 is MQA; 1 < K < N with K \mid N is grouped-query, with group size G = N/K.
Read the formula for what shrinking K actually buys. It touches only the K term, so the projection cost falls from 2N to N + K — at most a factor of two, and usually far less. That is not why anyone uses GQA. The payoff is the KV-cache, which scales with K alone and is the binding constraint at generation time.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Dot-product attention costs 12BT^2NH FLOPs in training. At what sequence length does it start to dominate the matmul FLOPs, and why that number?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Past T > 8D. With the usual proportions F = 4D, D = NH, N = K, the ratio of attention to everything else is
\frac {12BT^2NH}{18BTDF + 24BTDNH} = \frac {12BT^2D}{72BTD^2 + 24BTD^2} = \frac {T}{8D}
What that means in practice. At D \approx 8\mathrm {k} attention only takes over past roughly 64k tokens; Gemma-27B, with D = 4608, crosses at about 37k. Larger models push the crossover further out, so the quadratic term is not what stops large models training on long context — the KV-cache at inference is a much earlier wall.
The 12BT^2NH is two matmuls, QK^{\top } and SV, each 6BTSNH and each batched over B and the head axis.

fr:title.text: The KV cache scales with K, and is per-sequence

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The KV cache scales with K, and is per-sequence

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How large is a KV-cache, and which dimension actually drives it?

html:div.html:details:
Answer The cache has shape [2, S, L, K, H] per sequence — the leading 2 is keys and values — so in int8 it is 2SLKH bytes.
Worked: S = 8\mathrm {k}, L = 64, KH = D = 8192 gives 2 \cdot 8192 \cdot 64 \cdot 8192 \approx 8 GiB for a single sequence.
Two things in that expression decide inference planning. It scales with K, the number of key/value heads, and not with the N query heads — which is the whole argument for Group Query Attention and MQA at K \ll N. And it is per sequence, so unlike the weights it cannot be amortised over the batch: it competes with batch size for the same High bandwidth memory budget, and generation is bandwidth-bound on streaming it.

fr:title.text: Remat buys memory with a third more FLOPs

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Remat buys memory with a third more FLOPs

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What does block-level gradient checkpointing cost, and what does it save?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Saves: only the input to each layer is kept — one checkpoint per layer instead of the roughly twenty intermediate nodes a layer produces. In the book's setting (BT = 4M, L = 64, D = 8192, bf16) that is 84 TB of activations down to 4.2 TB.
Costs: the forward pass is run a second time inside the backward pass, so training goes from about 6 \cdot \mathrm {params} \cdot \mathrm {tokens} to about 8 — a third more FLOPs for a twentyfold cut in activation memory.
Why twenty nodes. Backpropagation needs whatever the derivative mentions. For f(x) = \exp (g(x)) we have df/dx = \exp (g(x)) \cdot dg/dx, so both g(x) and \exp (g(x)) have to survive to the backward pass. Counting every such intermediate across a layer lands around twenty.
The middle setting is usually the right one: save just the outputs of the big matmuls — about seven per layer — and no large matmul is ever recomputed, only the cheap elementwise work between them.

fr:title.text: The running max makes the chunk merge exact

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The running max makes the chunk merge exact

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In flash attention, what running statistics travel between KV chunks, and how are two chunks merged?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Each query block carries three: M, the running maximum of q \cdot k; L, the running softmax denominator; and O, the running output.
Merging chunks with local maxima M^1, M^2 and sums L^1, L^2 rescales each to the shared maximum:
L = e^{M^1 - \max (M^1, M^2)}L^1 + e^{M^2 - \max (M^1, M^2)}L^2
This is exact, not an approximation. It is only \sum _i e^{a_i + b} = e^b \sum _i e^{a_i}: pulling a constant out of a sum of exponentials. The maximum is subtracted for numerical stability and put back by the same identity — see Online Softmax for the one-pass version of the argument.
The payoff is memory, not FLOPs. The [B,T,S,N] attention matrix is never materialised, so memory is O(1) in the number of chunks while the FLOP count stays quadratic. The query block sits in VMEM and only the KV chunks stream in, which is also what raises the arithmetic intensity.

fr:title.text: Sparsity sets the batch an MoE needs

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Sparsity sets the batch an MoE needs

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A Mixture of Experts (MoE) has E experts and top-k routing, int8 weights on a TPU v5e (ridge point around 240 FLOPs/byte). What batch size does it need to be compute-bound, and what is that for DeepSeek v3?

html:div.html:details:
Answer B > 120E/k tokens. For DeepSeek v3, with E = 256 routed experts and k = 8, that is B > 3840 tokens — a startlingly large batch to require at generation time.
Per weight matrix: a full batch touches every expert, so all E copies get loaded — EDF bytes — while only k experts fire per token, so the work is 2kBDF FLOPs. The arithmetic intensity is therefore
\frac {2kBDF}{EDF} = \frac {2kB}{E}
and int8 weights against bf16 arithmetic need that above roughly 240, giving kB/E > 120.
The framing that makes this obvious: an MoE is a dense model with E MLP blocks per layer. Total parameters scale with E; parameters activated per token scale with k. The sparsity E/k — typically 8 to 64, and 32 for DeepSeek v3 — is exactly the factor by which the required batch inflates. The other cost is routing: two AllToAlls per MoE block, out to the experts and back.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A grid of processing elements in which every operand moves by one hop per cycle to a fixed neighbour, and nothing is addressed. A PE multiplies what arrives at it, adds what arrived from above, and passes the result on. There is no register file to name, no arbitration, and no scheduler: the dataflow is the wiring, and the only freedom in the design is which of the three operands you decide to hold still.

Hold the output still and each PE owns one entry of the result, accumulating in place while both inputs stream past. Hold the weights still — the choice the Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU) makes — and each PE pins one w_{ij} for the whole tile while activations stream in from the left and partial sums fall downward. The second is the one worth being able to draw from memory, because the staggering it requires is where every systolic-array bubble comes from:

The stagger is the whole trick. Row i of the activation tape is held back i cycles, so that x_k arrives at PE(k, j) on precisely the cycle the running sum for column j reaches that row. The set of PEs firing on cycle t is therefore the anti-diagonal i + j = t, and a finished dot product falls out of the bottom of column j having been accumulated on the way down — never written to memory, never read back.
What you pay for that is the fill and the drain. An N \times N array streaming M samples is busy for M + 2N - 2 cycles but does only M N^2 useful multiply-accumulates, so utilisation is

For the four-by-four array above, four samples give 40%. On a real 128 \times 128 MXU the fill is 2N - 2 = 254 cycles, so one isolated 8 \times 128 tile — the shape of the native op — would run at 8/262, near three per cent. That number is not what the hardware achieves, and the gap is the point: consecutive tiles stream in back-to-back with no bubble between them, so the fill is paid once per run of matmuls rather than once per tile. This is the fill bubble, and it is why the cost of a small matmul is dominated by a fixed charge that a large one amortises away.

This covers the math behind the online softmax algorithm required by Flash Attention (v1).
The first thing we must consider is numerical precision. Namely, the original softmax operation is given by
However, when operating with low precision data types (i.e. float16) the maximum value is 65536. Therefore, with \exp we can easily get numerically overflow.

To get around this, the online softmax algorithm adheres to the safe softmax. For safe softmax, we simply multiply the numerator and denominator by \exp (-m), where m = \max \{x_{1}, \ldots , x_n\}. This gives
Since x_i - m \leq 0, this ensures that each \exp (x_i - m) is bounded in a safe range.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Problem. Note that computing the \max over \mathbf {x} means that we must have all of the logits in a row of QK^T materialized in SMEM, or first loop over all of them to compute the max before computing the normalization constant.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The online softmax algorithm fuses the max reduction into the normalization pass, so a single sweep over the row suffices to compute the normalization with the max. The key difficulty is that the denominator depends on n for each i i.e.

Therefore, we must find a recursive relationship such that d_{i+1} = f(d_i, m_i, x_{i+1}) for some function f. This would then allow us to locally compute d_{i+1} with only the local information of current x_{i+1} and the two running statistics d_i and m_i. This is exactly the kind of algorithm that is conducive to memory tiling.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Question. What is f(d_i, m_i, x_{i+1})?

html:div.html:details: Answer.Consider d_{i+1} = d_i \cdot \exp (m_{i} - m_{i + 1}) + \exp (x_{i + 1} - m_{i + 1}).

Proof. This can be seen by directly rewriting d_{i + 1}.
\begin {align*} d_{i + 1} &= \sum _{j = 1}^{i+1} \exp (x_j - m_{i + 1}) \\ &= \left (\sum _{j = 1}^{i} \exp (x_j - m_{i+1})\right ) + \exp (x_{i+1} - m_{i+1}) \\ &= \left (\sum _{j = 1}^{i} \exp (x_j - m_{i})\right )\exp (m_{i} - m_{i + 1}) + \exp (x_{i+1} - m_{i+1}) \\ &= d_{i} \exp (m_{i} - m_{i + 1}) + \exp (x_{i+1} - m_{i+1}) \end {align*}

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The running denominator d is rescaled by e^{m - m_{\text {new}}} each time a new maximum is found, keeping it consistent with the safe-softmax shift.

html:pre.html:code: m = float("-inf") # running max of the logits d = 0.0 # running softmax denominator for i in range(n): # one fused sweep for the stats m_new = max(m, x[i]) d = d * exp(m - m_new) + exp(x[i] - m_new) m = m_new p = [exp(x[i] - m) / d for i in range(n)] # second pass: normalized probs

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Unfortunately, we cannot get around the second pass to compute the normalized output for \mathbf {p}. However, this is not the case in Flash Attention (v1).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Unlike in the online softmax, we are not interested in the outputted probability vector \mathbf {p}. Instead we are interested in the entire output matrix O given by
For more details see self-attention.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Notation. In correspondence with the notation in the online softmax, we define the following: x_{i,j} = \mathbf {q}_i \cdot \mathbf {k}_j, where \mathbf {q}_i is the ith row of Q and \mathbf {k}_j is the jth row of K. Similarly, \mathbf {o}_i is the ith row of the output matrix O given by \mathbf {o}_i = \sum _{j = 1}^{n} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_n)}{d_n} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Now following the template provided by the online softmax, we must find a recurrence for \mathbf {o}_i. Namely, we will consider the sequence \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' given by \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' = \sum _{j = 1}^{k} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j, such that \mathbf {o}_{i,n}' = \mathbf {o}_n
fr:mainmatter.html:div:
Claim. We have the following recurrence for \mathbf {o}_{i,k}':
\mathbf {o}_{i,k}' = \mathbf {o}_{i, k-1} \cdot \frac {d_{k - 1} \cdot \exp (m_{k-1} - m_{k})}{d_k} + \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_k

html:div.html:details:
Proof. We will proceed by directly rewriting the recurrence for \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' as
\begin {align*} \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' &= \sum _{j = 1}^{k} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j \\ &= \left (\sum _{j = 1}^{k - 1} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_{k-1})}{d_{k-1}} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j\right ) \frac {d_{k - 1} \cdot \exp (m_{k-1} - m_{k})}{d_k} + \frac {\exp (x_{i,k} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_k \\ &= \mathbf {o}_{i, k-1} \cdot \frac {d_{k - 1} \cdot \exp (m_{k-1} - m_{k})}{d_k} + \frac {\exp (x_{i,k} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_k .\end {align*}

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Thus, we are left with the following algorithm

html:pre.html:code: for i in range(N): # one query row at a time m = float("-inf") # running max of the logits d = 0.0 # running softmax denominator o = zeros(head_dim) # running output accumulator for j in range(M): # stream over keys/values x = q[i] @ k[j] # logit x_{i,j} m_new = max(m, x) d_new = d * exp(m - m_new) + exp(x - m_new) o = o * (d * exp(m - m_new) / d_new) + (exp(x - m_new) / d_new) * v[j] m, d = m_new, d_new out[i] = o

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. A key benefit of this algorithm is that it is entirely parallelizable across rows. This means that we can loop across entire tiles like in the GEMM case.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The forward pass of flash attention avoids materializing the N \times N attention matrix by streaming an online softmax. The backward pass has to pull the same trick twice over, because the naive gradient computation wants two N \times N matrices — \mathbf {P} and d\mathbf {P}. Getting there means first writing down every gradient we need, then finding a way to recompute rather than store each one.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Notation. Following the notation in the original paper, \mathbf {S} = \mathbf {Q} \mathbf {K}^T, \quad \mathbf {P} = \mathrm {softmax}(\mathbf {S}), \quad \mathbf {O} = \mathbf {P} \mathbf {V}, where \mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, \mathbf {V}, \mathbf {O} are N \times d and \mathbf {S}, \mathbf {P} are N \times N. For a scalar loss \phi we abbreviate the gradient with respect to any matrix \mathbf {X} as d\mathbf {X} = \frac {\partial \phi }{\partial \mathbf {X}}, and write \mathbf {L}_i for the softmax denominator of row i saved by the forward pass, so that \mathbf {P}_{ij} = \exp (\mathbf {Q}_i \cdot \mathbf {K}_j) / \mathbf {L}_i.

Componentwise, from \mathbf {O}_{ik} = \sum _j \mathbf {P}_{ij} \mathbf {V}_{jk},
That last line is worth noting already: d\mathbf {V} never needs \mathbf {P} stored, only the ability to re-evaluate \mathbf {P}_{ij} from \mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, and \mathbf {L}.

Collecting those scalars into a column \mathbf {D} with \mathbf {D}_i = \mathbf {P}_i \cdot d\mathbf {P}_i recovers the matrix form
\mathbf {D} is the piece that will cause trouble later: it is a dot product over an entire row of \mathbf {P}, which is exactly the thing we refuse to materialize.
One more chain rule, and the sums run over opposite indices:

Every gradient above is expressed through \mathbf {P}_{ij} and d\mathbf {P}_{ij}, both N \times N. Materializing either one is exactly the quadratic memory cost the forward pass went to such lengths to avoid, so the backward pass has to be able to produce those entries on demand.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Insight. Both are recoverable from the N \times d tensors already resident in memory. The forward pass saved \mathbf {L}, so \mathbf {P}_{ij} = \frac {\exp \left (\mathbf {Q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {K}_{j}\right )}{\mathbf {L}_{i}}, and d\mathbf {P} is just an inner product of two rows, d\mathbf {P}_{ij} = \sum _{k} d\mathbf {O}_{ik} \mathbf {V}_{jk} = d\mathbf {O}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {V}_j. Neither ever requires an N \times N intermediate.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Substituting both into the previous section leaves d\mathbf {Q} and d\mathbf {K} in terms of \mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, \mathbf {V}, d\mathbf {O}, \mathbf {L}, and \mathbf {D} alone:

One problem survives. \mathbf {D}_i = \mathbf {P}_i \cdot d\mathbf {P}_i is a dot product over a full row, so computing it inside the streaming loop would mean a reduction over all j before any tile of d\mathbf {Q}_i could be finished. This is the same global dependency the online softmax was designed to break.
The way out is that the row sum has already been computed once, in the forward pass. Expanding and pulling d\mathbf {O}_i out of the sum:

The inner sum is precisely the definition of \mathbf {O}_i. So \mathbf {D} is a single elementwise product of d\mathbf {O} and \mathbf {O} summed along the head dimension — one O(Nd) pass over tensors we already have, done once before the backward loop begins.
Forward pass. Store \mathbf {O} and the softmax denominators \mathbf {L}, both O(Nd).
Between the passes. Receive d\mathbf {O} from the layer above (automatic in JAX), then precompute \mathbf {D}_i = d\mathbf {O}_i \cdot \mathbf {O}_i in O(N) memory.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Problem. In this paper, they aim to address the problem of agentic kernel generation or as we refer to it: vibe compilation. Specifically, they target CUDA and raw PTX as a backend.
Technical challenges. There are many issues that arise in vibe compilation. A non-exhaustive list of challenges is as follows:

html:ul.html:li: Reward Hacking: A very common theme for any reinforcement learning based approach. In particular, see this paper for some examples of agents hacking KernelBench.

Synchronization errors: Even given a list of input output examples to check against, we cannot possibly determine whether there is an underlying race condition that appears rarely enough to pass the checks.
This seems to be a main focus of things like TIRx, where they hope to check these things at the IR level.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Core contribution. They develop CAKE IR, which is an intermediate representation for writing CUDA kernels. More importantly, they have the agent co-design the IR while trying to generate kernels. This is an iterative process, where the agent must implement existing kernels in its own designed IR. To do so, requires adding necessary features to the IR like Warp Specialization along with the corresponding lowering passes.

A refinement of the Test-and-set lock that reduces coherence traffic during the spin. Threads first perform a plain load to check whether the lock looks free, and only attempt the atomic test_and_set when it does. Spinning is then read-only, so cores can share the cache line.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: HBM Bottleneck. The default XLA attention does not fuse the softmax with the logit computation, requiring the entire logit matrix to be written back to HBM.
Vector Unit Limitations. MXU can be left idle while VPU is performing copmlex exponential and sum operations.
VMEM Residency and Loop Control. Pallas allows you to control data movement, so that we can explicitly enforce online softmax rather than writing back to HBM.
Temporal Control via LLO. Pallas also allows control over the temporal flow, preventing the compiler from reordering your manual optimizations.

html:ul.html:li: Inside the kernel, data has already been moved from HBM to VMEM.
If data exceeds VMEM, we need to tile with BlockSpec.
Also need to pipeline i.e. while doing computation on a given block, we need to be moving the next block from HBM to VMEM.
By default, pipelining is done for you, but there are other APIs to control this(?)
For-Loop scheduler.
Asynchronous overlap.
Buffer reuse. Uses same VMEM buffer across iterations.
Macro-tiling: this is done by Pallas / user. You define the larger software blocks i.e. 1024x1024 to hide latency DMA transfers. Pallas manages pipeling.
Micro-tiling: this is done by compiler / hardware. Translates larger block into hardware native VREG 8x128.
VLOAD: fetching inputs for chunk (8x128)(N + 1)th from VMEM and move to VRegs
VALU: Perform elementwise operations for current (Nth) chunk
VSTORE: write completed result for previous (N - 1)th chunk from VRegs back to VMEM.
Each block does a local softmax calculation.
Tracks a shared maximum and adjusts results.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Can Now fuse score calculation, softmax, and value aggregation into single pass.
No longer need to store NxN attention matrix in HBM.
Can break Q, K, V into small blocks that fit in VMEM.
Kernel available here.

html:ul.html:li: Dynamic scaling (\alpha ): Computes e^{m_{prev} - m_{next}} to track change in maximum logit across blocks for numerical stability.
Re-scale accumulation: Multiplies by \alpha to the previously accumulated sums before adding current block output to accurately rescale all past results.
Additive updates: partial results (current softmax and outputs) are added to running totals via fast multiply and addition ops.
Delayed normalization: only divide by normalization once at the very end of the loop because division is slow.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Block-size tuning. to maximize compute-to-load ratio need biggest block sizes that fit into VMEM.
With certain masks (i.e. causal) can skip alot of computation for parts of the attention matrix that are being masked out.

html:ul.html:li: Finer blocks -> can skip more but then have poorer utilization.
Sparsity pruning: Divide mask into blocks and discard all inactive blocks (all zeros).
Data compression: see how many unique mask patterns are needed to describe the remaining active blocks.
Execution map and pre-fetching: (active_rows, mask_next) generated to map the computation order and tell the MXU which mask pattern to prefetch for zero-latency application.
Block filtering (block_mask): categorizes QK blocks as zero, non-zero, partial.
Coordinate mapping (active_ros/cols): provides the hardware with (Q, KV) grid indices, ensuring efficient loading of active blocks from HBM.
Mask pipelining (mask_next): tells the hardware which mask pattern to prefetch.
SMEM-resident metadata: computed once per mask and stored in SMEM. Enable high-speed access to sparse execution map without need to re-transfer from HBM.
Grid definition: defined by (num_q_heads, grid_size). Grid size is set dynamically using the sparese meta data fwd_mask_info.num_active_blocks[0].
SMEM Inputs: num_scalar_prefetch instructs hardware to prefetch critical scalar/metadata inputs into SMEM before thread begins computing.
VMEM Inputs: (Q, K, V) that must be moved from HBM to VMEM for kernel to execute.
